money_at_stake.rationale: REVISED 2026-08-30 in the source-excerpt verification pass: two of the four original evidence items were deleted because their cited source did not support, or could not support, the claim. The White House fact sheet was cited for 'Proclamation 11002 ... effective 2026-01-15,' but the fact sheet, fetched twice this run with targeted searches for 'January 15', 'Proclamation 11002', '11002', '12:01', 'effective date', 'will take effect', gives no proclamation number and no effective date anywhere on the page; it states only that the action was taken 2026-01-14. Techtimes.com (the Phase 2 reporting citation) returned HTTP 403 on refetch and the Wayback Machine is unreachable from this session, so it could not be opened at all. Neither item was repaired with a substitute source. What survives: GingerControl's compliance analysis, reconfirmed verbatim on refetch, that Phase 1's own exemptions (100+MW US data centers, R&D, startups, repairs, non-data-center consumer and industrial use, public sector) mean 'the practical impact falls on a narrow slice of commercial imports that do not qualify for these carve-outs' -- no dollar figure is published for that narrow current base. And CCIA's own dated economic analysis (2026-06-11), reconfirmed verbatim on refetch, modeling what removing that exemption would cost: an effective 15.6% tax on data-center construction, USD 450bn in capex and GDP lost across 2026-2030 (about USD 90bn a year) against a McKinsey baseline of USD 2.7 trillion in total planned 2025-2030 US data-center capex, 20% of planned buildouts affected, with softer carve-out variants costing USD 16-45bn a year. A direct follow-up question to that same CCIA source on refetch confirms its paper names no active Commerce Department review, no decision deadline and no announced proposal to remove the exemption: it reads as a preemptive advocacy argument, not a response to a live process. It is nonetheless on-topic and dated: it is the industry's own published economic case in the same live fight over this exemption that this occurrence describes, and every one of its published annual figures, from the softest carve-out (USD 16bn) to full removal (USD 90bn), clears the USD 10bn floor for B10_100 while staying under the USD 100bn floor for GT_100B. Banded B10_100 on that basis, with the limit stated plainly: the actual current dutiable base is unquantified and narrow per GingerControl, and the larger figure is an industry-modeled scenario, not a confirmed policy outcome.

evidence.claim: The tariff applies to chips classifiable under HTSUS subheadings 8471.50, 8471.80, or 8473.30, but semiconductors imported for use in U.S. data centers above 100 MW are exempt, and broad exemptions for data centers, startups, R&D operations, and public sector applications mean 'the practical impact falls on a narrow slice of commercial imports that do not qualify for these carve-outs.'
evidence.source_name: GingerControl, Section 232 Semiconductor Tariff: Rate, HTS Codes and Exemptions
source_excerpt: Products are subject to the 25% tariff if they are classifiable under HTSUS subheadings 8471.50, 8471.80, or 8473.30.
Semiconductors imported for use in U.S. data centers above 100 MW are exempt under HTS 9903.79.03.

However, broad exemptions exist for U.S. data centers, startups, R&D operations, and public sector applications, meaning the practical impact falls on a narrow slice of commercial imports that do not qualify for these carve-outs.

evidence.claim: Applying the tariff to data centers by removing the current exemption would impose an effective 15.6% tax on data-center construction, costing about USD 450bn in capex and GDP between 2026 and 2030 (about USD 90bn a year) against a McKinsey estimate of USD 2.7 trillion in total planned 2025-2030 US data-center capex, affecting 20% of planned buildouts; softer carve-out variants of the same policy cost USD 16-45bn a year.
evidence.source_name: CCIA, Applying Semiconductor Tariffs to Data Centers Would Cost the U.S. $90 Billion a Year
source_excerpt: Applying 25% Section 232 semiconductor tariffs to data centers would represent a 15.6% tax on data center construction.
A 15.6% tax on data center construction would lead to the relocation, cancellation or delay of about 20% of planned 2026-2030 data center buildouts in the U.S.
This would cost the U.S. about $450 billion in capex and GDP between 2026-2030, or about $90 billion per year.
McKinsey projects U.S. data center capital expenditures will reach $2.7 trillion between 2025 and 2030.
GDP loss falls to roughly $16 billion annually, jobs at risk to approximately 43,000.
GDP loss to $45 billion annually, and jobs at risk to roughly 122,000.

public_reach.rationale: Split with a large non-investable share, for a reason distinct from the Arctic precedent (there the money went to sanctioned or state operators; here a chunk of it does not go to anyone at all). Of the CCIA figure that anchors the money leg, 20% of planned data-center buildouts being affected is forgone capex, not a pool any issuer captures; the tariff actually collected is revenue to the US Treasury, which is the state side of the same test method already applies to sanctioned or state-owned operators. What remains reachable is genuinely mixed: the buyers absorbing higher landed cost are mostly listed hyperscalers and OEMs, the chip vendors the White House fact sheet names as the tariff's target are listed (NVIDIA, AMD), but the entities positioned to newly capture value, advanced-packaging and OSAT houses that could onshore the last assembly step, and customs-classification and compliance shops that navigate the threshold, are a mix of listed and mostly-private names this appraisal has not sized. REVISED 2026-08-30: the evidence item citing a possible Phase 2 widening of the payer base to listed device OEMs was deleted in the source-excerpt verification pass; its source, techtimes.com, returned HTTP 403 on refetch and the Wayback Machine is unreachable from this session, so it could not be opened. The score is unchanged because the deleted item was a supporting nuance, not the basis for the split-reach finding itself. Not scored at 60 because the two biggest components of the CCIA figure, forgone GDP/capex and government tariff revenue, reach no listed issuer at all; not scored at 15 because a real, named, partly-listed complex of payers and compliance beneficiaries exists and a chain build would be the way to size it.

evidence.claim: 20% of planned 2026-2030 US data-center buildouts would be affected by removing the exemption, against a USD 2.7 trillion McKinsey baseline for total planned capex; this is framed as capex that does not happen, not capex that moves to another balance sheet.
evidence.source_name: CCIA, Applying Semiconductor Tariffs to Data Centers Would Cost the U.S. $90 Billion a Year
source_excerpt: A 15.6% tax on data center construction would lead to the relocation, cancellation or delay of about 20% of planned 2026-2030 data center buildouts in the U.S.
McKinsey projects U.S. data center capital expenditures will reach $2.7 trillion between 2025 and 2030.

evidence.claim: The proclamation and fact sheet name NVIDIA H200 and AMD MI325X, both listed issuers, as the chips the tariff was written around.
evidence.source_name: The White House, Fact Sheet: President Donald J. Trump Takes Action on Certain Advanced Computing Chips
evidence.source_excerpt: The President also imposed a 25% tariff on certain advanced computing chips, such as the NVIDIA H200 and AMD MI325X.

capture_odds.rationale: Mostly a cost or tax pass-through rather than a profit pool, with a narrow real exception. The dominant flow behind the money leg, forgone data-center capex and government tariff revenue, does not convert into profit for any market participant by construction. The commercial response this exact mechanism has already produced once, when a hard TPP-and-bandwidth threshold met Nvidia's export-control line, was redesigning the chip (the H20) rather than paying and passing the cost through, which is evidence that firms facing this tariff's identical threshold shape will spend engineering effort to avoid the tax rather than generate a margin pool for someone else to capture. The one segment where money could plausibly stick is the second-order one Nell's card names as the real unmapped question: last-assembly-step onshoring and customs classification. That segment is real (advanced packaging is genuinely qualification-gated capacity, and firms are already investing in US packaging capacity for adjacent reasons) but its size relative to the headline figure is not published anywhere I found, so it is scored as a real but small exception rather than the main case. Not scored at 15 because that packaging and classification exception is concrete and named, not scored above 40 because the tariff's own design incentive is demonstrably to engineer around the tax rather than pay it into anyone's margin. Evidence unaffected by the 2026-08-30 verification pass; both items were refetched and reconfirmed verbatim, score unchanged.

evidence.claim: The H20 was engineered specifically to fall below the same style of TPP-and-DRAM-bandwidth threshold that this tariff uses, evidence that chipmakers respond to a hard performance threshold by redesigning under it rather than paying and passing the cost through a supply chain.
evidence.source_name: SoftwareSeni, How the 25 Percent AI Chip Tariff Actually Works and What It Means for GPU Procurement
evidence.source_excerpt: The H20 was engineered to fall below export control thresholds — TPP and DRAM bandwidth are cut significantly.

evidence.claim: The tariff's own exemption design is conditioned on 'the buildout of the U.S. technology supply chain and the strengthening of domestic manufacturing capacity,' i.e. it is structured to reward onshoring rather than to raise revenue from a stable tax base, which cuts against a durable margin pool forming around the current design.
evidence.source_name: The White House, Fact Sheet: President Donald J. Trump Takes Action on Certain Advanced Computing Chips
evidence.source_excerpt: This tariff will not apply to chips that are imported to support the buildout of the U.S. technology supply chain and the strengthening of domestic manufacturing capacity for derivatives of semiconductors.

timing_fit.rationale: Scored 40 on 2026-08-30 in a second repair pass, after refetching a primary document the deleted evidence never actually rested on and finding one new source the prior pass never located. The proclamation's own operative text, opened directly at GovInfo.gov's Compilation of Presidential Documents (the certified GPO archive of Proclamation 11002 itself, a different and more authoritative page than the White House fact sheet the deleted item cited and that page could not support), states in Clause 3: 'This tariff shall be effective ... on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern standard time on January 15, 2026.' That is this occurrence's own anchor_date exactly, fetched and quoted verbatim this run. It settles the specific defect that forced the deletion: the base tariff mechanism's own timing is not in doubt, and it has already been live for over seven months as of this as_of date. That alone does not put the LARGE money on a schedule. GingerControl's own analysis (money_at_stake evidence, unchanged by this pass) already establishes that the currently dutiable base under this live mechanism is 'a narrow slice of commercial imports,' and the CCIA figure that actually put money_at_stake into B10_100 rests on removing the current data-center exemption, a scenario CCIA's own 2026-06-11 paper does not tie to any announced government process (money_at_stake rationale, unchanged). What is new since that June paper, and since the earlier deleted techtimes.com item: MoneyCheck, refetched this run and itself summarizing POLITICO's reporting, quotes a 'Politico report based on conversations with eight informed sources' describing an internal Commerce Department mechanism that would mean 'elimination of exemptions that were part of tariff measures announced in January,' naming the same data-center exemption CCIA models removing, dated 2026-08-27, three days before this appraisal. That is real, fetched, on-topic movement toward the exact scenario the money leg is priced on, independently corroborated in substance by other outlets converging on the same POLITICO-derived account the same two days (Tom's Hardware, Benzinga, TrendForce, freepressjournal, all dated 2026-08-27/28), which is a materially stronger basis than the single broken techtimes.com citation this leg previously rested on and lost entirely. It is scored well short of 60 because the same MoneyCheck source states plainly that 'the entire policy framework remains fluid and could undergo major modifications in the weeks and months ahead' and that 'neither the White House nor the Commerce Department provided immediate responses to media inquiries regarding the proposal': nothing here is confirmed, dated, or committed, it is anonymously-sourced reporting of an internal discussion, not an announced rule, a docketed review, or a stated deadline. Not scored at 15 or left NULL because the reporting is fresh, multiply corroborated, and squarely on the same exemption the money leg already prices on, which is real timing-relevant evidence and not a manufactured number. Net: the base mechanism is certainly and already inside the window; the scenario that sets the size of the money is credibly in motion but has no committed date, so this leg lands at 40 rather than the 60 'credible inside the window' anchor or the 80 this appraisal briefly carried before the source-excerpt pass.

evidence.claim: Proclamation 11002 states the tariff on covered advanced computing chips is a 25 percent ad valorem duty rate effective with respect to goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern standard time on January 15, 2026, which is this occurrence's own anchor_date.
evidence.source_name: GovInfo.gov (U.S. Government Publishing Office), Compilation of Presidential Documents, Proclamation 11002: Adjusting Imports of Semiconductors, Semiconductor Manufacturing Equipment, and Their Derivative Products Into the United States
source_excerpt: Proclamation 11002—Adjusting Imports of Semiconductors, Semiconductor Manufacturing Equipment, and Their Derivative Products Into the United States

Except as otherwise provided in this proclamation, imports of Covered Products will be subject to a 25 percent ad valorem duty rate. This tariff shall be effective with respect to goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern standard time on January 15, 2026, and shall continue in effect, unless such action is expressly reduced, modified, or terminated.

evidence.claim: Politico reporting based on conversations with eight informed sources describes internal Commerce Department discussion of eliminating the exemptions attached to January's semiconductor tariff, including the data-center exemption; the White House and the Commerce Department did not confirm this, and the reporting itself describes the policy framework as fluid with no set timeline.
evidence.source_name: MoneyCheck, Trump Administration Eyes Sweeping Tech Tariffs Targeting Semiconductors and Electronics
source_excerpt: Elimination of exemptions that were part of tariff measures announced in January. The earlier exemptions applied to data centers, research and development activities, startup companies, consumer-facing applications, and government sector applications.
Politico report based on conversations with eight informed sources
the entire policy framework remains fluid and could undergo major modifications in the weeks and months ahead.
Neither the White House nor the Commerce Department provided immediate responses to media inquiries regarding the proposal.

notes.text: Correction to the occurrence's own framing: Nell's economic_impact dimension (score 80) reads 'it taxes the bill of materials of every US AI data center build.' Independent verification finds the opposite is written into the rule as of this appraisal: Phase 1 explicitly exempts imports for qualifying 100+MW US data centers, which is why an independent trade-compliance analysis calls the actual dutiable base 'a narrow slice of commercial imports.' The reason this still bands B10_100 rather than THIN or LT_1B is not the current rule, it is that the same proclamation's own review clock produced, four days before this appraisal, reporting that the administration is weighing removing exactly that exemption as a Phase 2 move, and an industry group has already published a dated dollar model of what that would cost (USD 16-90bn a year). A chain build here should treat Phase 1 and a possible Phase 2 as two different sized occurrences and should start from the packaging and customs-classification link Nell flagged as unmapped, since that is the one place in this chain money plausibly sticks rather than passing through to a government treasury or simply not being spent.

Follow-up to the note above, after the same-day source-excerpt verification pass: the 'administration is weighing removing exactly that exemption as a Phase 2 move' claim in that note rested on a techtimes.com citation that could not be reopened (HTTP 403) and has been deleted from timing_fit and money_at_stake. A direct refetch of the CCIA source also confirms its own paper names no active government review or decision deadline; it is a preemptive advocacy argument, not a report on a live process. money_at_stake stays B10_100 because CCIA's own published figures clear the band's USD 10bn floor regardless, but the 'live Phase 2' urgency asserted above is no longer something this file can stand behind, and timing_fit is now NULL rather than 80.

timing_fit repair pass: the effective-date claim was never actually false, it was cited to the wrong document. The White House fact sheet the earlier pass fetched is a summary page and genuinely does not name a proclamation number or an effective date; the proclamation itself, on GovInfo.gov's certified Compilation of Presidential Documents, does, in its own operative Clause 3, verbatim, fetched this run. Separately, a fresh WebSearch (not a rescue of the dead techtimes.com link) surfaced MoneyCheck's 2026-08-27 summary of POLITICO's reporting on an internal Commerce Department push to eliminate the January exemptions, fetched and quoted this run: real, dated, on-topic, and independent of the item that was deleted. Neither item overrides money_at_stake's or capture_odds's or public_reach's rationale, which are unchanged; the tension the new MoneyCheck item creates with money_at_stake's 'CCIA's paper names no active government review' line is real and is noted here rather than by editing that leg: CCIA's paper is dated 2026-06-11, before this Aug-27 reporting existed, so the two are not in conflict, they are sequential.
